articles.title: Corridor raises $25M seed to build a health benefits brokerage for SMBs | TechCrunch
articles.text:
It’s been a while since Jackson Wagner left his job as a product lead at Scale AI in July 2022. Now, he’s building in a new space altogether: The new effort is an AI health benefits brokerage called Corridor that focuses on small businesses, which it says traditional brokerages often overlook because small accounts generate lower commissions even though they take the same amount of time as larger accounts.
Corridor is betting an AI solution may help on that front. On its platform, customers work with human advisors while AI agents do administrative tasks in the background. The company says its agents can handle tedious office work like checking whether a doctor is in a customer’s insurance network, scheduling care, or providing a doctor updated health insurance information.
“We are every single employee and management’s concierge for all things healthcare,” Nikhil Aggarwal, the company’s CEO, told TechCrunch.
On Monday, Corridor said it had raised a $25 million seed round led by Bain Capital Ventures.
Corridor came about after Wagner was in a running accident, and the poor handling of his care led him down a path of “significant, consistent, chronic pain.”
“I developed a long list of complications that needed to be worked through one by one,” he said.
He eventually left Scale AI to get a master’s degree in computer science and electrical engineering at UC Berkeley, before joining Build Robotics in 2023. Later, he teamed up with former Scale AI colleague Eric Qian to work on Capernaum AI, a startup building a clinical agent targeting musculoskeletal care and chronic pain.
The two eventually approached Cold Start to see if they would fund Capernaum, but Aggarwal, who was a partner at Cold Start along with Jason Dong, saw a much larger opportunity. So the four of them took off and launched Corridor together.
“Since health plans are the window through which the vast majority of Americans access healthcare, it became overwhelmingly clear that one of the highest impact things I could do to improve outcomes for individuals was to create a way for them to access better health plans,” Wagner said.
Other companies in this space include Ignition Benefits and Nava Benefits.
Investors in Corridor’s round include BoxGroup, as well as executives from OpenAI, Scale AI, and Ramp. The startup is now preparing for Q4, since “80% of small businesses choose their health plan in Q4,” Aggarwal said.
“Our vision is to build the most trusted healthcare institution in America,” he said. “To earn that, we are laser-focused on a simple promise: doing what we say we’re going to do for the businesses and employees we serve.”

articles.title: GM can’t ‘bring back’ Apple CarPlay because it never left
articles.text:
Last week, GM announced a new software experience for its upcoming Chevy Silverado and GMC Sierra trucks, including a new look for Apple CarPlay and Android Auto, the popular phone mirroring systems that the automaker made a big deal about removing from its electric vehicles in 2023.
GM can’t ‘bring back’ Apple CarPlay because it never left
The recent reveal of GM’s new software interface in its trucks has left some people confused about the automaker’s stance on phone mirroring.
Naturally, this led to some confusion about whether GM was “bringing back” CarPlay and Android Auto to its vehicles. Yahoo Finance reported it that way, calling it an “about-face” by the automaker, while Apple Insider’s headline boasted that GM “cave[d]” on its decision to remove the interface from its gas-powered vehicles. Even The Verge’s own commenters were a bit flummoxed about what was going on.
It’s certainly true that GM has not offered phone projection in any of its electric vehicles for the past three years. That means no CarPlay or Android Auto in the Chevy Equinox, Blazer, Bolt, and Silverado EVs; Cadillac Lyriq, Optiq, Vistiq, and Escalade IQ; or GMC Sierra and Hummer SUV and Truck EVs.
All of those vehicles have Google software products embedded in their systems, like Maps and Gemini. That’s because GM builds its operating system on top of Android Automotive, which is often called Google Automotive Services or GAS when bundled with the full suite of native apps. But if you’re hoping to plug in your phone, or connect wirelessly, and see the familiar app layout on the infotainment screen of a GM electric vehicle, you’ll be sorely disappointed.
The same can’t be said about GM’s many gas-powered trucks and SUVs. GM never disabled phone projection in its best-selling ICE models. Tens of thousands of owners of GM-branded vehicles regularly project their phones’ displays on their vehicles’ infotainment screens without any issue. And now CarPlay and Android Auto are both getting spiffy new picture-in-picture upgrades in the Chevy Silverado and GMC Sierra, a sign that perhaps GM is learning to co-exist with phone mirroring.
GM is partly responsible for the confusion. In an October 2025 appearance on Decoder, GM CEO Mary Barra defended the company’s decision to prohibit CarPlay in its electric vehicles and indicated that the policy would eventually extend to GM’s gasoline-powered lineup as well.
Everyone freaked out for a second time. Removing phone projection in EVs was one thing, but many truck and SUV owners were understandably incensed about the prospect of losing the capability in their beloved GM-branded vehicles. But a few days later, GM seemed to walk back that statement, clarifying to a number of outlets that Apple CarPlay and Android Auto would remain available in its gas-powered vehicles “for the foreseeable future.” Last week’s announcement of a new software experience in the Silverado and Sierra trucks would seem to be included in that “foreseeable future.”
Allow me to add some further reporting here. For the Silverado/Sierra announcement, I spoke to Colin McCormick, group product manager for Google built-in, projection, and profiles at GM. Here’s what he had to say about how GM’s position on phone projection has evolved over the years:
And so the way that I look at this is that we were one of the early adopters of CarPlay and Android Auto when it first came out. And we do have a small segment of EVs right now that don’t offer that, but there is a large majority of our vehicles that do offer that. And our big position on this is that it shouldn’t be two competing systems. So as we work together with Apple and Google to provide solutions that we think are best for the customer, this is what we’re representing in this new UI design. So I think we’re landing in a spot where … we don’t have a customer that has to decide, ‘Oh, I’m going to use projection,’ or, ‘Oh, I want to use the native system.’ That’s our sweet spot for us. And that’s where we want to live.
GM most likely realizes that its position on CarPlay and Android Auto isn’t popular. People really like mirroring their phones! It’s clean, it’s familiar, and it’s (mostly) dependable. The same can’t be said for most modern cars’ native software. Even the ones that are really well designed, like Rivian and Tesla, still struggle with some core functions like profile logins and messages. And you can find plenty of owners of both brands that would give their firstborn child for the ability to mirror their phone.
CarPlay and Android Auto aren’t perfect. They have dependability problems and connectivity problems aplenty. But they are worlds better than the majority of the native operating systems in cars today — most of which are just trash. Yes, they’re getting better. And GM is not wrong in thinking it can offer a better experience. But people get testy when you take away their choices.
So GM is finding ways to coexist with CarPlay and Android Auto. It doesn’t want to lose more customers over it, which is why we’re getting this most recent solution that includes picture-in-picture phone projection. GM thinks this solves the “two competing systems” problem, as mentioned by McCormick. But what it really does is get it out of the corner it backed itself into over phone mirroring.

articles.title: Cài phần mềm trái phép, bị phạt 15 triệu đồng
articles.text:
TPO - Ngày 19/9, Phòng An ninh chính trị nội bộ Công an TPHCM cho biết, cơ quan này vừa ra quyết định xử phạt Công ty L.A. 15 triệu đồng do sao chép, cài đặt phần mềm máy tính trái phép tại một trường học trên địa bàn thành phố.
Công ty L.A có trụ sở tại phường Phú Thọ Hòa, TPHCM, do ông P.L.H. làm người đại diện theo pháp luật.
Theo Công an TPHCM, doanh nghiệp này bị xử phạt về hành vi “sao chép tác phẩm mà không được phép của chủ sở hữu quyền tác giả”, quy định tại điểm a, khoản 2, Điều 16 Nghị định số 341/2025/NĐ-CP ngày 26/12/2025 của Chính phủ về xử phạt vi phạm hành chính trong lĩnh vực quyền tác giả, quyền liên quan.
Bên cạnh mức phạt 15 triệu đồng, cơ quan chức năng yêu cầu Công ty L.A thực hiện các biện pháp khắc phục, tiêu hủy và gỡ bỏ những bản sao vi phạm.
Trước đó, Công ty L.A được xác định đã sao chép, cài đặt trái phép phần mềm máy tính tại một trường học trên địa bàn TPHCM. Công an thành phố nhận định vụ việc là lời cảnh báo đối với các tổ chức, cá nhân trong việc sử dụng phần mềm và các tác phẩm được bảo hộ quyền tác giả.
Theo cơ quan công an, tùy tính chất và mức độ, hành vi xâm phạm quyền sở hữu trí tuệ có thể bị xử lý bằng ba hình thức.
Trường hợp chưa đến mức truy cứu trách nhiệm hình sự, tổ chức hoặc cá nhân vi phạm có thể bị xử phạt hành chính. Chủ thể quyền sở hữu trí tuệ cũng có quyền khởi kiện ra tòa án, yêu cầu bên vi phạm xin lỗi, cải chính công khai và bồi thường thiệt hại. Đối với hành vi đủ yếu tố cấu thành tội phạm, người vi phạm có thể bị truy cứu trách nhiệm hình sự theo Điều 225 hoặc Điều 226 Bộ luật Hình sự.
Từ vụ việc trên, Công an TPHCM khuyến cáo các tổ chức, cá nhân không thực hiện hoặc tiếp tay cho hành vi sao chép, phân phối, sử dụng tác phẩm và phần mềm trái phép. Trước khi cài đặt hoặc đưa phần mềm vào sử dụng, đơn vị cần kiểm tra nguồn gốc, giấy phép và phạm vi quyền sử dụng để tránh vi phạm pháp luật.
Cơ quan công an nhấn mạnh, tôn trọng quyền tác giả và quyền sở hữu trí tuệ là một trong những điều kiện góp phần xây dựng môi trường số văn minh, an toàn và phát triển bền vững.

articles.title: AI model costs are pushing startups towards cheaper open weights
articles.text:
Harvey’s gross margin fell from about 50% at the start of this year to minus 50% by June as customer usage of its AI agents spiked, and turned positive again only after it released a model of its own built on Moonshot’s Kimi K3. Abridge, Decagon, Ramp and Rogo are making similar moves, and Sequoia Capital and General Catalyst are funding the shift.
Harvey’s gross margin fell from about 50% at the start of this year to minus 50% by June, Bloomberg reported, citing a person familiar with the matter. The legal startup is valued at $15.6B. Customer usage had spiked after a March update to its AI agents.
The cost was the models it rented.
Harvey has seen a twentyfold rise in token usage this year, according to the company. Both OpenAI and Anthropic now charge enterprises for model usage on top of base subscription fees. Its founders knew the spike would not survive contact with those rates.
So it stopped renting.
In August Harvey released its first in-house model, post-trained on Kimi K3 from the Chinese lab Moonshot. Gross margins turned positive again after that launch and other changes to how it uses AI, people familiar with the work told Bloomberg. Harvey declined to comment on specific financials.
It is not alone.
Abridge is building a clinical model on Nvidia’s open weights, and Decagon now routes 80% of customer queries through models of its own. Ramp raised $750M in June and is weighing training for the first time. “It made absolutely no sense a year ago,” co-chief executive Karim Atiyeh said. “It’s starting to make a lot more sense now.”
Anthropic has noticed.
At an investor forum in its offices it showed a slide on startups building their own models, with a reminder that Harvey still needs Opus for its hardest tasks. Mistral’s Arthur Mensch spent July arguing that closed models give providers immense leverage, and named Anthropic cutting off Windsurf while building Claude Code.
September made his case for him.
OpenAI moved to end its Cursor contract after SpaceX bought the company, citing past terms of service breaches by Musk businesses. European buyers have switching rights under the Data Act, but those cover a customer leaving a supplier, not a supplier leaving a customer.
Europe has its own Harvey.
Legora, in Stockholm, reached $100M in revenue inside 18 months and now serves more than 1,200 firms, and it has never said whose models it runs on. Not everyone thinks the answer matters. “Having your own model or not is such the wrong question,” said Menlo Ventures partner Matt Kraning. “In most cases, it tends to be a lot of cosplay.“

articles.title: What to consider when buying an Ethernet switch for your home network - Engadget
articles.text:
What to consider when buying an Ethernet switch for your home network
The right Ethernet switch can add ports without slowing your network or saddling you with features you don't need.
If you're running out of Ethernet ports, that doesn't mean you need another router. If your Wi-Fi coverage is already working well, an Ethernet switch is the simpler option to connect additional PCs, game consoles, TVs, network-attached storage and other wired devices.
However, shopping for an Ethernet switch gets complicated quickly. There are five-port and eight-port models, Gigabit and multi-gig options, and managed switches with settings that most people will never use. Buying the one with the most numbers on the box doesn't mean it will be the best for you. The best approach is picking a switch that will accommodate your existing network and leave room for future devices.
Start with the number of Ethernet ports and their speed
The port count is the simple part, though there is a catch. Typically, you'll use one port to connect the switch to your router, leaving four ports for other devices on a five-port switch. If you need four more ports right now, an eight-port switch (with room for seven devices) gives more breathing room for future devices.
Speed takes a little more thought. If your internet connection, router and wired devices all max out at Gigabit speeds, then a 1GbE switch is perfectly reasonable. If you have multi-gig internet, a newer PC with 2.5GbE or a fast NAS with multi-gig networking, then a 2.5GbE switch makes more sense. It also avoids jumping up to pricier 10GbE hardware if you don't really need that.
What's vital is that the switch shouldn't become the bottleneck. If the router has a 2.5Gbps port and the switch is limited to 1GbE, the traffic between the router and switch will be limited to 1GbE. The same applies at the other end: plugging a device with a 1GbE port into a 2.5GbE switch doesn't magically make it faster.
Internet speed isn't the whole story, either. Two 10GbE-capable devices connected to the same 10GbE switch can move files across your local network much faster than your internet plan allows, which can matter for large NAS backups or video files. And 2.5GBASE-T can run over existing Cat5e cabling, so moving beyond Gigabit doesn't necessarily mean rewiring the house.
Most homes don't need a fully managed switch
For a lot of homes, an unmanaged switch is all you need. These add more ports without requiring any configuration. Just plug one into your router, hook up your devices and get on with your life. You can even use methods to wire in more devices without Ethernet.
Managed and smart switches typically cost more and provide you with greater control. Features can include virtual LANs (VLANs), traffic monitoring, quality-of-service controls and other device separation or management tools. These can be useful if you're creating a complex home network. But if you don't need these features, there's no reason to pay extra for a settings page you never visit.
Another feature to consider is Power over Ethernet (PoE). PoE can transmit power and data over the same Ethernet cable, which is especially helpful for security cameras and Wi-Fi access points. But you have to do more than only counting the PoE ports. Switches have an overall PoE power budget, meaning that a model with multiple PoE ports may not have sufficient wattage to operate all devices at their maximum power simultaneously. Check what your devices need, what each port can provide and the total budget available across the switch.
The boring physical details matter as well. A small fanless switch will blend in next to a TV or on a desk, while larger models with active cooling make more sense tucked away with the rest of your networking gear.

articles.title: SPX Express đầu tư hạ tầng, mở rộng mạng lưới điểm dịch vụ toàn quốc
articles.text:
Logistics Việt Nam đang bước vào giai đoạn phát triển với quy mô ngày càng lớn. Theo Bộ Công Thương, thị trường dịch vụ logistics hiện đạt khoảng 45 - 50 tỷ USD, tương đương 10% GDP, với tốc độ tăng trưởng bình quân 14 - 16% mỗi năm. Chính phủ cũng đặt mục tiêu duy trì tốc độ tăng trưởng ngành 12 - 15%/năm, đưa logistics trở thành một ngành dịch vụ hạ tầng quan trọng của nền kinh tế giai đoạn 2025 - 2035, tầm nhìn đến 2050.
Trong đó cần kể đến chiến lược tập trung thúc đẩy đầu tư, hình thành các trung tâm logistics quy mô lớn, hiện đại tại các vùng kinh tế trọng điểm; đồng thời ưu tiên hạ tầng phục vụ thương mại điện tử, kho thông minh hướng tới tối ưu chi phí vận tải và nâng cao hiệu quả chuỗi cung ứng.
Định hướng này cũng thúc đẩy các doanh nghiệp logistics không chỉ nâng cao năng lực xử lý, mà còn mở rộng mạng lưới và khả năng kết nối để đáp ứng tốt hơn nhu cầu của thị trường. Đây cũng là những trọng tâm mà SPX đã và đang thực hiện, trong đó các trung tâm khai thác, phân loại quy mô lớn đóng vai trò là nền tảng xử lý, còn hệ thống bưu cục cùng đội ngũ giao hàng hiện diện tại khắp các khu vực đảm nhiệm vai trò kết nối, vận chuyển đến người dùng và doanh nghiệp trên toàn Việt Nam.
Xây dựng hạ tầng quy mô lớn và nền tảng năng lực xử lý
Khi nhu cầu vận chuyển ngày càng mở rộng, năng lực xử lý tại các trung tâm phân loại đóng vai trò quan trọng trong việc luân chuyển bưu kiện hiệu quả giữa các khu vực. Vì vậy, việc đầu tư vào các trung tâm quy mô lớn, ứng dụng tự động hóa không chỉ nhằm gia tăng công suất, mà còn giúp nâng cao khả năng xử lý, điều phối và luân chuyển hàng hóa một cách hiệu quả.
Theo hướng này, SPX đang từng bước củng cố và mở rộng hạ tầng trên toàn quốc với các trung tâm phân loại hàng hóa quy mô lớn được đầu tư tại những khu vực trọng điểm ở cả phía Bắc và phía Nam.
Ở phía Bắc, từ năm 2023, SPX đã đưa vào hoạt động trung tâm phân loại hàng hóa tự động tại Khu công nghiệp Việt Nam - Singapore (VSIP) Bắc Ninh. Với diện tích 100.000 m², trung tâm có khả năng xử lý lên đến 5 triệu bưu kiện mỗi ngày. Trong khi đó, tại Hưng Yên, SPX đang xây dựng trung tâm mới được định hướng trang bị hệ thống phân loại tự động thế hệ mới với công suất dự kiến xử lý lên tới 7 triệu bưu kiện mỗi ngày khi đi vào hoạt động.
Tại Bình Dương (nay thuộc TP.HCM), SPX đang hoàn thiện trung tâm phân loại tự động. Sau khi đi vào hoạt động, đây sẽ là trung tâm phân loại tự động lớn nhất của SPX ở khu vực phía Nam.
Những khoản đầu tư này góp phần củng cố năng lực xử lý của SPX, kết hợp với công nghệ tự động hóa giúp đáp ứng sản lượng bưu kiện ngày càng tăng và nâng cao tính ổn định trong vận hành toàn mạng lưới.
Mở rộng điểm chạm với khách hàng sử dụng dịch vụ
Năng lực logistics còn nằm ở khả năng đưa dịch vụ đến gần người sử dụng. Với khách hàng, một mạng lưới chỉ thực sự thuận tiện khi việc gửi và nhận hàng có thể diễn ra gần nơi họ sinh sống, làm việc hoặc kinh doanh.
Để gia tăng khả năng tiếp cận khách hàng, SPX đã mở rộng và nâng cấp hơn 100 bưu cục trên cả nước tại TP.HCM, Hà Nội, Hải Phòng, Lạng Sơn, Quảng Ninh,... Các bưu cục được bố trí tại những khu vực thuận tiện để người dân tiếp cận dịch vụ vận chuyển dễ dàng hơn.
Song song với hệ thống bưu cục và mạng lưới sẵn có, SPX còn mở rộng độ phủ dịch vụ thông qua việc kết hợp với các điểm giao nhận đối tác. Từ năm 2025, doanh nghiệp triển khai chương trình Đối tác điểm giao nhận, bổ sung thêm các điểm kết nối để người dùng có thể gửi hàng trực tiếp, lựa chọn lấy hàng tận nơi, giao hàng tận nơi hoặc gửi hàng tại điểm để nhận sau.
Mạng lưới các điểm giao nhận này đáp ứng nhu cầu vận chuyển ngày càng đa dạng, từ hộ kinh doanh gửi đơn cho người mua mỗi ngày, cửa hàng luân chuyển sản phẩm giữa các địa điểm, đến nhu cầu gửi đồ, quà tặng cho người thân, bạn bè ở tỉnh, thành phố khác.
Chiến lược mở rộng đồng thời các trung tâm phân loại quy mô lớn, đầu tư tự động hóa, phát triển bưu cục và bổ sung các điểm giao nhận không chỉ đơn thuần nhằm mở rộng mạng lưới. Đây còn là cách SPX xây dựng một hệ thống logistics có nhiều lớp kết nối chặt chẽ khi các trung tâm phân loại lớn tạo năng lực xử lý ở phía sau, còn hệ thống bưu cục cùng đội ngũ giao hàng hiện diện tại khắp các khu vực đảm nhiệm vai trò kết nối, vận chuyển đến người dùng và doanh nghiệp trên toàn Việt Nam.
Khi thị trường logistics Việt Nam được kỳ vọng tiếp tục duy trì tốc độ tăng trưởng hai chữ số trong những năm tới, năng lực cạnh tranh của doanh nghiệp sẽ ngày càng phụ thuộc vào khả năng xây dựng hạ tầng đủ lớn, mạng lưới đủ rộng và dịch vụ đủ linh hoạt. Với SPX, quá trình đầu tư vào hạ tầng và mở rộng điểm chạm đang hướng đến một mô hình logistics có khả năng phục vụ rộng hơn, tiến tới đáp ứng các nhu cầu gửi - nhận hàng hóa thường xuyên và đa dạng của người dùng trên cả nước, nhất là trong dịp cao điểm cuối năm.

articles.title: I Printed a Shovel, Earrings, and Everything in Between With This 3D Printer
articles.text:
Easy for anyone to use. Consistently perfect prints. Enclosed chamber for temperature control. New tool-free nozzle-swap feature. AMS add-on makes multicolor printing a breeze.
TIRED
Speed causes a lot of shaking—needs a very stable surface to sit on. Filament waste disposal makes a mess. Fumes from high-temperature filaments are still very intense.
Does the average consumer actually need a 3D printer? Isn’t it just for people who want to sell fidgets at the flea market, design obscure brackets in CAD, or print groups of Warhammer figurines?
Yes, they do, and no, it isn’t.
Photograph: Kat Merck
In my four weeks of testing the Bambu Lab P2S Combo, I have printed a sponge holder for my kitchen sink; caps and parts for my hydroponic gardens; various clips and hangers; a Mason jar lid organizer; a shovel; a couple of funny signs; plant pot coasters; a shoehorn; truck bed tie-downs; a pair of earrings; and, of course, a Benchy—every piece perfectly smooth and looking like it was purchased from a store. Owning a 3D printer is like having an Amazon fulfillment center right in your house.
While I'm no stranger to 3D printing—I owned the open-frame Bambu Lab A1 before I started testing 3D printers—I have never used a machine as easy to operate as the P2S. In fact, when we reviewed Bambu Lab’s P2S predecessor, the popular and bestselling P1S, earlier this year, tester Brad Bourque declared it the easiest-to-use 3D printer he’d ever tried, claiming its lack of complicated steps and futzing has changed the way he thinks about 3D printing.
The P2S builds on the already excellent P1S design with a new 5-inch color touchscreen, tool-free nozzle swapping, a beefed-up 1080p 30-frames-per-second camera with improved AI failure detection, and a redesigned airflow system. I wasn’t exactly in love with the latter, but one complaint for a system with thousands of failure points is more than enough to earn the P2S a solid A-grade.
Detail of identical pigeon figurine printed on white Bambu Lab PLA: A1 on left, P2S on right.
Photograph: Kat Merck
Photograph: Kat Merck
It Really Is That Easy
If you own another brand of mid- or lower-tier 3D printer, any Bambu Lab machine will already feel like an upgrade. Much like an iPhone, any Bambu Lab printer will work seamlessly right out of the box, with easy-to-use software and intuitive design elements. With a little assembly, you’re ready to go.
The large touchscreen allows you to perform many functions and troubleshooting right on the machine. These printers are easy for even the most clueless newbie to use and understand—so much so that some call the company “the Apple of 3D printing.” (Even better, the company’s free, flagship Bambu Studio software is open source.)
What makes both the P1S and P2S worth the upgrade from the A1 is the enclosed chamber that provides environmental control for acrylonitrile filaments like ASA and ABS, which require high temperatures to melt and are notoriously prone to warping. In the P2S, Bambu Lab incorporates a new airflow system that switches modes depending on the filament—it pulls in cooler air for more easily melted PLA, or retains air (and therefore heat) for ASA and ABS.
However, I did notice that when printing in ASA (note that the P2S comes with only a rough-textured build plate; I had to buy the smooth $30 engineering plate separately), the resulting fumes were overwhelming—I had to close the door, open the windows, and turn on an air purifier. There is a carbon filter in the back of the device, but during high-heat prints, the airflow is supposed to circulate inside the unit; instead, it seemed to leak out around the door and other cracks.
Video: Kat Merck
Fumes are emitted from all 3D printers, so this is not really a flaw on the company’s part, just an indication that the redesigned airflow system has room for improvement. Make sure you keep the printer in a room with a door that can close if you’re printing with any kind of impact-modified plastics. Bambu Lab’s helpful Wiki also offers a 3D-printable exhaust kit that can redirect fumes outside.
And speaking of locations, you will also want to ensure the 15 x 16 x 19-inch P2S is on a very firm surface—perhaps even on the ground. At 600 mm per second, the nozzle moves vigorously, which will shake whatever it’s on. I was using a low wooden table, but since I found myself using the printer near-daily, the shaking eventually loosened the table’s leg joints, resulting in multiple X-Y axis error messages on the machine. Research showed this to be a somewhat common issue, almost always resolved by finding a firmer surface.
I was not able to test the AI failure detection, as none of my 30-plus prints failed (aside from a couple of mismeasurements on my end), but I did have occasion to view through the 1080p camera—if you download the free Bambu Handy app, it will store a little time-lapse video of your object being printed, which is fascinating to watch.
In Living Color
The “Combo” in the name refers to the Automatic Material System (AMS) that sits on top of the printer. (You can also buy it separately at $299.) It holds four spools of filament that auto-feed to your project—a game changer if you’re printing something with multiple colors. Without it, a multicolor print would necessitate stopping the print, removing the spool of filament, and installing a new one on the side. For the P2S, the AMS also has the ability to dry the filament—this removes any absorbed ambient moisture that would create steam when heated and mess up your print.
The AMS add-on allows for seamless multicolor prints.
Photograph: Kat Merck
I tested the P2S on the West Coast in late summer, when the humidity was very low, so my filament stayed below 40 percent relative humidity, according to the built-in hygrometer—it didn’t need drying. However, if you live in a humid region, springing for the AMS will be a massive time-saver.
With the P1S, if you needed to swap out a different nozzle, it was something of an ordeal—you basically have to unplug everything and take apart the assembly with screws. On the P2S, the front of the nozzle head is magnetic and pops right off—simply unclip the old nozzle and clip in the new one. Another massive improvement if you find yourself swapping nozzles often.
The P1S’s automatic nozzle cleaning function that “poops” filament blobs out the back of the machine is still in effect on the P2S. I’d been warned, but I was still surprised to see the amount of detritus it left on the floor, especially during multi-color prints. I highly recommend that a “poop chute” or collection basket be one of your first prints. (And there are plenty of fun designs for using the waste filament blobs once they’ve accumulated, from creative games to a “poop Atlas” filament waste world map.)
Do You Really Need One?
Yes, unless you need a dual-nozzle printer or a commercial-grade unit that can also laser cut and engrave—features this printer doesn’t offer. The ability to print and customize useful household and garage objects, art projects, and toys easily and quickly—with minimal fuss—makes the P2S worth every penny. This is doubly so if you have some basic engineering skills, as importing files into Bambu Studio is a cinch.
Bambu Lab-brand filaments start at about $15 a roll with spool. Note that we flagged some app inconsistencies when using non-Bambu filaments with the P1S, but I did not have any non-Bambu filaments on hand to test in the P2S, so I can’t vouch for whether this issue has been fixed.
While the P2S may well be overkill if you only want to print the occasional fidget or figurine, if you regularly find yourself in need of some annoyingly specific organizer, replacement cap, or bracket, this machine could well pay for itself over time in both convenience and material costs.
Kat Merck is a commerce editor for WIRED, where she covers smart bird feeders, indoor gardening systems, kitchen composters, and all things sustainable home tech. As a forestry major at California Polytechnic State University, San Luis Obispo, Kat practiced axe throwing on her college logging team and trained as a wildland firefighter ... Read More

articles.title: Paramount settles lawsuit blocking $110 billion Warner Bros. merger
articles.text:
Paramount has reached a settlement with California and the 11 other states that sued to block its planned $110 billion acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery. The settlement removes a major roadblock standing in the way of the massive media merger.
Paramount settles lawsuit blocking $110 billion Warner Bros. merger
This settlement will resolve the antitrust lawsuit filed by California, New York, Washington, and several other states to block Paramount’s big deal.
According to the proposed consent decree filed with the court, it includes requirements like minimum numbers of theatrical film releases over the next five years, starting with 30 in years one and two and 32 in the following years, and a commitment to spend at least $300 million more on production in the US compared to what the companies spent in 2025. At least four of the films produced must be independent films, and at least 20 percent must be “tentpole” blockbuster movies with $50 million-plus budgets and releases on a minimum of 3,000 US screens within the first month.
If Paramount doesn’t meet these film release requirements, it must divest Miramax Studios and pay $30 million per missed film. It also requires the merged company to keep offering a free streaming service, like Pluto TV, and includes a commitment not to sell Paramount Studios or Warner Bros. lots in California for at least five years.
The settlement has rules for the negotiations over cable channels owned by the combined company as well, in addition to requirements for a news editorial independence board “made up of five established journalists” with at least 10 years of experience to ensure editorial independence at CBS and CNN. The Writers Guild of America also settled its antitrust lawsuit against Paramount.
At a press conference announcing the agreement, California AG Rob Bonta called the arrangement “the opposite” of the 2018 Disney-Fox deal, where Fox’s film output dropped afterward. “Let me be clear: This settlement is not a vote of support for this merger,” Bonta adds in a press release. “But we believe this settlement, which resolves our antitrust concerns in every market alleged in our case, protects competition and consumer choice, and puts workers’ needs, concerns, and futures first, is the best course of action.”
Paramount Chairman & CEO David Ellison:
We are grateful to Attorney General Bonta and his fellow AGs, as well as the WGA, for engaging in good faith to find a path forward to a resolution that serves all parties, and to Governor Newsom for his support throughout this process. Our shared aim was an outcome that best serves consumers, workers and — most importantly — the creative community so vital to the art of visual storytelling. We’re confident this agreement does exactly that, memorializing a series of commitments that include 30+ films annually and expanded U.S. film production to help revitalize our industry here at home.
Our goal has always been to build a stronger Hollywood — one with more stories told, greater choice for consumers and stronger competition. That vision was validated by unanimous approval from competition authorities in nearly 70 jurisdictions worldwide, who agreed this deal is pro-competitive, pro-consumer and pro-worker. Having now addressed the State AGs’ and WGA’s concerns, we have complete clearance for this merger and look forward to putting these commitments into action. Bringing Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery together will build that stronger Hollywood, creating expanded opportunity for our people and even more great entertainment for audiences around the world.
The settlement comes just days before Paramount’s “ticking fee” was set to go into effect, which would require the entertainment giant to pay WBD shareholders 25 cents per share for each quarter the deal is delayed past September 30th. The fee would’ve cost Paramount about $7 million per day.
Though the Trump administration signed off on the $110 billion merger, California, along with Arizona, Colorado, New York, Washington, and others, sued Paramount and WBD in July over antitrust concerns. They claimed the megamerger would create a “media behemoth” that would “inflict substantial harm” on the entertainment industry. A judge granted the states’ request to pause the merger shortly after.

articles.title: How to use an iPad as a second screen for your Mac or Windows PC - Engadget
articles.text:
How to use an iPad as a second screen for your Mac or Windows PC
Your iPad can give your Mac or PC some much-needed extra screen space.
Portable displays can be quite useful for boosting your productivity on the go, and your iPad can pull double duty as one. It wasn't exactly designed to work as an external monitor, but it actually works really well for that purpose. Maybe you're working from a coffee shop or traveling, and all you have with you is your Mac and iPad. From third-party apps to Apple's own solution, there are many ways to turn your iPad into a monitor. Not only that, but they also enable features like Apple Pencil support on your Mac. It all depends on your setup and the features you need.
Sidecar: the built-in option for Mac
Sidecar is the simplest route, but there are a few requirements you need to meet. The most important one is having a Mac. Windows users are out of luck here, although there are alternatives in that case. If you already have a Mac, you're ready to go. From there, both devices need to be on the same iCloud account. It won't work if you use different accounts on your devices, so check your iPad Settings before continuing.
If your iPad and Mac are already signed in to the same account, using Sidecar is easy. On your Mac, open Control Center — it's the icon with two toggle switches in the Menu Bar. Look for Screen Mirroring, the two overlapping squares, in the list. Choose your iPad, and it turns into a secondary display for your Mac. From there it acts like any external display with full resolution and adjustable placement. You can even go to the Display settings under System Settings to rearrange the iPad's screen however you like.
iPad and Mac users also have access to Universal Control. Instead of turning the iPad into an external display, the idea is to use inputs from one device to control the other. Move the Mac's cursor onto the iPad's screen, send input the other way or even drag and drop between the two devices. Like Sidecar, both devices must be on the same iCloud account. Two-factor authentication has to be on, too. It works with pretty much every Mac and iPad released in the last few years.
If that doesn't work for you for some reason, try manually enabling Universal Control in the Screen Mirroring settings in Control Center. Look for Display Settings. Click "+" and select your iPad from the Link Keyboard and Mouse list.
Alternatives for Windows users
There are apps that replicate Sidecar's features on Windows too. Duet Display is one of the most popular ones, and it offers even more controls than Apple's Sidecar. It also runs on Mac, useful if your Mac and iPad aren't on the same Apple ID. But while Sidecar is completely free, Duet Display requires you to pay for a license. Also, you need to install the app on both your PC and iPad. It's an extra step Mac users skip, but a minor one. Open the app on both devices and you're set.
Luna Display, for Mac and Windows, works differently. It relies on a companion dongle that you plug into your computer first. This dongle handles the wireless transmission and makes it more reliable. Plus, Luna doesn't require a subscription — you pay $79 for the dongle, and that's it. It's good for those who hate being tied to a recurring subscription. Another big plus over other solutions is that Luna Display has a "headless mode." Plug the dongle into a Mac mini and use it directly with your iPad. No monitor needed.
Duet Display, Luna Display and Sidecar let you control macOS using the iPad's touchscreen. You can even use your Apple Pencil for navigation and drawing, turning your iPad into a graphics tablet. The Mac's own mouse and keyboard keep working the whole time. The experience is largely seamless, though glitches do turn up now and then. Keep in mind using a wired connection can help reduce these issues. Also, having the right iPad accessories — like a nice stand — can take your Sidecar experience to the next level.

articles.title: Hyundai's answer to the EV slowdown is building tens of thousands of robotaxis
articles.text:
Hyundai will build tens of thousands of Ioniq 5 robotaxis for Waymo at its plant in Georgia, chief executive Jose Munoz said, calling robotaxis the biggest new opportunity inside a slowing electric market. In Europe the only type approval route that works across the whole union for a fully automated car is capped at 1,500 units a year per vehicle type.
Hyundai will build “tens of thousands” of Ioniq 5 robotaxis for Waymo at its plant in Georgia, chief executive Jose Munoz told an event in San Jose, InsideEVs reported. He said the robotaxi manufacturing business is already profitable, and is becoming “a business unit on itself“.
The reason is the electric slowdown.
With the US tax credit and fuel economy rules gone, carmakers have taken large write-downs on electric assets. Where rivals “decided to write down their assets, we decided to make the most out of our assets“, Munoz said. Hyundai adjusted Savannah to build more hybrids and fewer electric cars.
Robotaxis are where the electric volume went.
Waymo runs about 4,000 vehicles across 14 US cities. The first Ioniq 5s not meant purely for testing arrive this quarter, built with redundant steering and braking and fitted with Waymo’s sixth-generation system at a plant in Arizona. Hyundai also builds Ioniq 5s for Motional, its own autonomous arm.
Hyundai is also the option that is not Chinese.
Waymo’s cheaper purpose-built robotaxi, the Ojai, has its bodies built by Zeekr in Ningbo and shipped to Arizona as stripped shells to keep the tariff bill down. A Georgia-built Ioniq 5 does not need that arrangement. Morgan Stanley puts the finished Ojai at about $125,000.
Europe cannot take these numbers.
The only approval route that works across the whole union for a fully automated car is capped at 1,500 units a year per vehicle type. Tens of thousands is not a European figure under that rule.
National approvals exist, and they stop at borders.
Waymo is going to Munich under the German framework for level four services passed in 2021, and is targeting late 2027 for commercial rides. It will spend the intervening period mapping the city and driving it manually. Germany passed the first level four commercialisation framework in the world.
That is one city, under one country’s law.
Munoz said there is “a lot of interest” from other customers and that he sees “a significant opportunity to scale up“. The scaling he means is American. Europe’s version of the same ambition runs at 1,500 cars a year per model.

articles.title: Justice for CSS
articles.text:
The first S in CSS stands for “style.” Think colors and fonts, borders and shadows, rows and columns, animations and transitions. CSS is the programming language that makes a website look pretty (or pretty ugly, often). It’s what makes this very webpage look like itself—look WIRED.
One paragraph in, a certain reader will already be smarting at my description of CSS. “It’s a style sheet language,” I can hear them say, “not a programming language.” (The second S indeed stands for “sheets,” and the C, if anyone cares, for “cascading.”) Or, “it’s a domain-specific language, not a general-purpose language.” Also, “it doesn’t execute” and, of course, “it’s not Turing complete” (although … ). Granted, CSS is a little different. There’s no compile step, and it doesn’t throw errors at run time like other languages. But that’s all beside the point.
The gatekeeping over whether CSS is a “real” programming language exists partly because it’s so simple to start—anyone can grok “background: red” right away. But simple does not mean easy, as the programmer-writer Jeremy Keith observed, and calling CSS easy or unserious should be tired by now. There were about 50 properties in the initial CSS specification in 1996 (like “color” and “font-size”); today there are at least 10 times as many (get ready for “hanging-punctuation”). The language has changed so much in three decades, and by now it is just so capable. One programmer recently re-created Doom in CSS. Others have used it to build holographic Pokémon cards and 3D-rendering engines. Cassidy Williams, who competed in this year’s inaugural March MadCSS tournament, built an experimental database-query engine entirely in CSS. When she demo’d it at Microsoft Build, even the emcees—seasoned programmers themselves—took a cheap shot at CSS. “You’re one of the people that likes it,” they snarked. “You might be the only one.”
Why is the lore of JavaScript’s creation so famous (Brendan Eich, Netscape, 10 days) and yet hardly any programmer would recognize the name of CSS creator Håkon Wium Lie? It might have something to do with Lie being a Norwegian guy with a diacritic in his name, not an American in Silicon Valley like Eich nor a Brit like Tim Berners-Lee, who invented HTML. And to be fair, JavaScript and HTML each have a chip on their own shoulder to worry about. But in the browser’s holy ternary of JavaScript-HTML-CSS, people tend to treat CSS as less than or purely decorative. Styling can be decorative—and wonderfully so—but the legibility and rich design it affords are important. People care how things look!
There’s another, uglier explanation for the CSS disrespect: It’s considered a “feminine” language. CSS developers work on the frontend—the part of a website you can actually see. There’s the obvious undertone that dealing with style and beauty is Female Work, along with the recycled joke that a CSS developer is “a freak in the style sheets.” How seriously a language is taken has knock-on effects on programmer salaries, what skills are sought out and tested in job interviews, and how accessible websites are for people with disabilities.
I recently talked to a friend, a talented backend engineer, about this. In college, she got an internship at a reputable software company in San Francisco doing entirely backend work. “I’d never expressed any interest in frontend at all, almost to an extreme extent,” she told me. “I don’t like frontend.” And yet, when she joined the company full-time after graduation, she was immediately assigned … a frontend role. She eventually worked her way back to the backend, and by now she’s used to the skepticism. “I’ve been in a million and one conversations with the classic man engineer who doesn’t think I know what I’m talking about until they work with me for six months and see my first backend project.”
I didn’t know this specific story when I first asked my friend if, maybe, I dunno, she had any experience with people assuming she was a CSS girlie. But the “coincidence” is really more of a probability. To overcorrect for such situations, she’s taken to branding herself as unmistakably backend-y. When we worked together, whenever it came time to distribute tasks among our team, she made it quite clear that she did not want to touch the frontend. (I don’t think we ever played Nose Goes, but that was the spirit.) I’d have been seriously obtuse to make the same mistake her manager did.
That same friend used to teach at Kode With Klossy, a tech camp for young women and gender-expansive students started by supermodel Karlie Kloss. Her experience there was all about the other, optimistic side of the coin: CSS can be a gateway into software for those who don’t fit the nerdy-computer-boy stereotype. “These girls would come in who had no interest in coding but just thought that Karlie Kloss was cool, and they would have so much fun,” she said. “They would grow to care more about, like, OK, how does this work?”
Within the industry, the Klossy approach is reflected in slightly better (but still really bad) gender diversity in front-of-the-frontend engineering jobs, compared to back-of-the-frontend and pure backend roles. Of a few thousand respondents in the State of CSS survey last year, 11 percent were women and 3 percent were nonbinary or gender-nonconforming. Pathetic, I know. But the State of JavaScript reported only 6 percent female and 1 percent nonbinary.
Another downstream consequence of CSS neglect is the sameness of websites across the internet, especially in Startup-land. If CSS is what makes a website look like itself, then the more recent fast fashion of frameworks is what makes them all look alike. There was a Bootstrap era, a Tailwind look, and now a distinctive Claudeslop aesthetic. Frameworks are athleisure, and if you’re not into fashion, they’re a shortcut to looking OK. Fair enough. But it does bum me out, in the same way the grayification of American cars bums me out compared to those old photos of technicolor parking lots.
WIRED was one of the first major, high-traffic sites to adopt CSS. It was a “Site for Your Eyes,” WIRED declared, and it was. But back then, there was no Flexbox nor Grid, no custom properties, and no @keyframes, transitions, and transforms for JavaScript-free animations. In this decade alone, so many powerful CSS features have landed in browsers that it’s hard to keep up. I’m no CSS expert, but I know enough to be past the overconfidence cliff in the Dunning-Kruger curve and into the valley of respect and reverence. I delight in one-off goodies like “text-wrap: pretty” (which prevents an orphan word stuck on its own line from ending a paragraph) as much as broad improvements like nested declarations. In the last few years alone, we got container queries, the :has() pseudo-class, and new color spaces like oklch(). CSS supports right-to-left languages, like Hebrew and Arabic. It interpolates positioning of the pieces of a web page to create buttery animations and gradients. And now, with if() conditionals and @function in development, even the “well, technicallyyy” explanations of why CSS isn’t a legit programming language might finally be put to rest. This is not your mother’s CSS.
The fact that CSS is simple to start, yet deep to explore and master, is part of why I love it so much. It’s the closest language we have to end-user programming, the idea that software should be customizable by any user. Style sheets are like spreadsheets in that way: A novice can build something useful in an hour, and experts can build fucking Doom.

articles.title: Không chỉ tuyển người giỏi, hãy xây dựng DN thành hệ thống tạo ra người giỏi
articles.text:
Người giỏi trên thị trường luôn hiếm, cán bộ quản lý giỏi còn hiếm hơn. Người giỏi và phù hợp lại hiếm hơn nữa. Nếu doanh nghiệp chủ yếu dựa vào tuyển dụng bên ngoài, doanh nghiệp sẽ phải liên tục cạnh tranh bằng lương, chức danh và đãi ngộ. Và mỗi khi một người giỏi ra đi, tổ chức lại phải bắt đầu một cuộc tìm kiếm mới.
Doanh nghiệp trưởng thành cần chuyển từ tư duy “săn người giỏi” sang “tạo ra người giỏi”.
Có thể hình dung quá trình này như một phễu nhân tài.
Miệng phễu là tuyển dụng. Doanh nghiệp vẫn phải có chuẩn đầu vào, nhưng không nhất thiết chỉ tuyển những người đã giỏi sẵn. Không cần quá khắt khe ở đầu vào, thậm chí có thể mở rộng để thu hút nhiều người có tiềm năng. Quan trọng là tuyển được những người có tiềm năng trở thành người giỏi. Họ chưa hoàn hảo nhưng có tư chất phù hợp, khả năng học hỏi nhanh, động lực vươn lên, thái độ tốt và phù hợp với các giá trị của tổ chức. Kiến thức và kỹ năng còn thiếu có thể đào tạo. Tiềm năng phát triển mới là thứ cần đặc biệt chú ý ở đầu vào. Không lọc người giỏi ngay từ đầu.
Nhưng tuyển đúng người có tiềm năng mới chỉ là bước đầu. Bên trong phễu mới quyết định doanh nghiệp có tạo ra được người giỏi hay không.
Con người phải được đào tạo, nhưng quan trọng hơn là được phát triển thông qua công việc. Từ việc nhỏ đến việc lớn, từ bài toán đơn giản đến bài toán khó, từ làm theo hướng dẫn đến tự quyết định, từ chịu trách nhiệm cá nhân đến dẫn dắt một nhóm người. Đào tạo cung cấp kiến thức. Công việc thực tế, thử thách và trách nhiệm mới biến kiến thức thành năng lực.
Trong quá trình đó phải có đánh giá và sàng lọc liên tục. Không phải tất cả những người bước vào miệng phễu đều đi đến cuối. Có người không phù hợp sẽ rời đi, có người dừng lại ở mức nhân viên giỏi, một số phát triển thành cán bộ quản lý, và chỉ một tỷ lệ nhỏ trở thành những cán bộ xuất sắc. Sự rơi rụng không phải thất bại của hệ thống. Sàng lọc chính là một phần của quá trình hình thành nhân tài.
Để chiếc phễu này hoạt động tốt, doanh nghiệp cần xây dựng hệ tri thức của mình. Quy trình, phương pháp, kinh nghiệm, dữ liệu, các tình huống thành công và thất bại phải được tích lũy và chuyển giao. Người mới đến không phải bắt đầu từ số không, mà được đứng trên nền tảng tri thức của những người đi trước để trưởng thành nhanh hơn.
Đồng thời, mỗi cán bộ quản lý phải có trách nhiệm phát hiện, đào tạo và tạo ra người kế nhiệm. Một giám đốc giỏi không chỉ là người tạo ra kết quả kinh doanh tốt, mà còn phải tạo ra những người có thể thay thế mình. Nếu một đơn vị chỉ hoạt động tốt khi người đứng đầu còn ở đó, tổ chức ấy, người CEO ấy chưa thực sự mạnh.
Như vậy, doanh nghiệp cần xây dựng cả một cỗ máy tạo ra người giỏi:
Tuyển người có tiềm năng → đào tạo → giao việc thật → thử thách → kèm cặp → đánh giá → sàng lọc → giao việc lớn hơn → hình thành người giỏi → hình thành cán bộ quản lý → tạo ra thế hệ kế nhiệm.
Khi cỗ máy ấy vận hành tốt, doanh nghiệp không còn quá phụ thuộc vào một vài ngôi sao và cũng không quá lo sợ khi một người giỏi ra đi.
Doanh nghiệp mạnh không phải là doanh nghiệp tuyển được nhiều người giỏi nhất. Doanh nghiệp mạnh là doanh nghiệp có khả năng liên tục biến người có tiềm năng thành người giỏi, biến người giỏi thành cán bộ quản lý giỏi, và biến cán bộ quản lý giỏi thành người tạo ra thế hệ giỏi tiếp theo.
Đó cũng là một năng lực tổ chức khó sao chép và là lợi thế cạnh tranh bền vững.

articles.title: Bungie says it’s “not done with Destiny” and will bring back vaulted content
articles.text:
Months after seemingly giving up on Destiny 2, Bungie now says it’s planning to restore vaulted content in the game like campaigns, destinations, and raids. The decision reverses the Destiny Content Vault that Bungie created six years ago, controversially removing older content from Destiny 2 that players had paid to access.
Bungie says it’s ‘not done with Destiny’ and will bring back vaulted content
Bungie is reversing its controversial content vault that saw Destiny 2 content removed six years ago.
“We understand that removing these experiences had a lasting impact on player trust and enjoyment of Destiny,” admits Bungie. “We cannot change the decision we made, but we can acknowledge its impact and do the work to make it right by restoring these important parts of Destiny’s history.“
All Destiny 2 players will get access to the vaulted content, but it’s not a simple switch of a button for Bungie. The developer made big changes to Destiny 2 with the Beyond Light expansion, meaning it has to go back and update lighting, encounters, combatants, and other underlying systems for this older content. “That work will take time, but it is necessary to ensure returning content meets the stability and gameplay standards of Destiny 2 today,” says Bungie.
The decision to return this content to Destiny 2 comes just weeks after a “Sunrise” Destiny 2 offline preservation mod appeared. The mod lets players access older areas in Destiny 2 that had been vaulted, but not the exact campaigns and missions that players had experienced previously.
Bungie now says its own restoration project is the “first step to lay the foundation for how we reforge into new stories and games that you all deserve.” Could that be a Destiny 3 sequel? There’s no mention of such a project, despite fans desperately pleading for a successor to Destiny 2 in multiple high-profile Twitch streams in recent weeks. Bungie is only committing to building a “stronger long-term future for Destiny” right now.
Alongside the Destiny 2 efforts, Bungie is also admitting that Marathon, its extraction shooter, didn’t “reach as many players as we had hoped, and we also know and understand that the game needs to evolve.” That means Marathon will expand deeper into a survival experience. The changes are a little vague right now, but it sounds like Marathon really needs to change and attract more players if it’s to be a sustainable project for Bungie.

articles.title: Don't throw away your old Android tablet — do this instead - Engadget
articles.text:
Don't throw away your old Android tablet — do this instead
Android Auto will run right on your tablet's screen with the Open Headunit app.
When a tablet gets old, it can often become nothing more than an expensive coaster. That's doubly true of Android tablets, which run the gamut from premium to ultra-budget in quality. Once they can no longer reliably run modern apps, Android tablets have few paths forward. They may be handy as e-readers or smart home control panels, but frankly you can probably find better ways to accomplish those tasks.
But one unexpected use for an Android tablet is as a head unit for Android Auto, using it to control your phone, navigate and play media on the go. Using the Open Headunit app, which costs just shy of $4 on the Google Play Store (though you can get it free from GitHub if you've got a bit more tech know-how), you can trick your phone into seeing your tablet as an Android Auto unit and displaying a big, car-friendly infotainment system right on the larger screen. It's not perfect, but after some extensive testing, I've concluded that it's a viable option for anyone whose vehicle doesn't support Android Auto by default, especially at a time when auto makers are increasingly halting Android Auto support.
Android Auto is a service that connects your phone with your car and displays a driving-friendly version of Android on your car's touchscreen infotainment system. It's a wonderful perk for drivers lucky enough to have a car that supports it, but many do not, especially older vehicles. If you're relying on a regular Bluetooth connection to your phone for navigation and entertainment, putting a tablet in your car as an Android Auto interface could be a significant upgrade.
Your tablet can become your car's infotainment system
Getting the Open Headunit app running requires some fiddling. It allows multiple connection types — USB, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth and running Android Auto directly on-device if your tablet supports it — and you'll need to do some experimenting to figure out which plays nice with your combination of hardware. Additionally, you'll need to connect the tablet to your car's audio system in order to play music or other media through it. Open Headunit has a handy built-in configuration tool that will walk you through all the most important settings and adjust them to work with your setup. Gemini in Android Auto is supported, too.
In my case, the issues with wireless Android Auto got me good, and USB ended up being the easiest solution. Once I spent some time enabling all the various permissions for Open Headunit and making it the default for USB connections, plugging my phone into my Samsung Galaxy Tab S10 Ultra would reliably open Android Auto and resume playback on my Spotify through its speakers. Connecting the tablet to my car's Bluetooth allowed the audio to pipe through my car stereo, but that created too much latency. I was able to reduce the delay by using a small USB-C hub with a 3.5mm headphone jack, then wiring an auxiliary cable from that into my car's own 3.5mm jack.
Performance was great on my tablet, but it's a high-end unit only a couple of years old. Unfortunately, I was not able to test Open Headunit on older hardware. My ancient Nexus 7 from 2013 got stuck in a boot loop when I dug it out of storage, and a Galaxy Tab S6 Lite from 2019 experienced a display malfunction. Neither recovered by filing time. With that said, all the processing for this test was done on my phone, with the Open Headunit app simply fooling the phone into thinking the tablet is a car.
Open Headunit isn't a perfect replacement for built-in Android Auto
You might not want to leave a tablet visibly mounted in your car at all times, as even an older tablet may be a tantalizing target for thieves who don't know any better. Personally, my tablet pulls double-duty as my primary computing device, so if I stick with Open Headunit long-term, I plan to install multiple MagSafe car mounts in a row on my dash and stick multiple magnet rings on the backside of my tablet, hopefully supporting the weight of the device while I drive and allowing me to easily toss it back into my bag when I park. Or maybe I'll just grab one of the many car tablet mounts available on Amazon. For now, the tablet sits propped in the tray area below the car's actual head unit when I'm running Open Headunit.
Clearly, this is not a perfect solution. But it's a lot cheaper than buying a new head unit for Android Auto, especially if you already have a tablet. If your car's stock head unit has quirks that make it particularly aggravating to replace, Open Headunit is a decent way to avoid that experience altogether. The head unit in my 2015 Subaru failed a couple of years ago, and it would cost me over $2,000 to get it replaced by an official dealer. I could buy my own Android Auto head unit and install it myself, but after looking up some guides, it's not something I'll have time for in the near future. I'm just not that much of a car guy. In the meantime, this solution works well enough. And I have to admit, Android Auto is a very luxurious experience on a 14.6-inch, 2K AMOLED display.

articles.title: Corridor raises $25m for an AI benefits brokerage
articles.text:
“For decades, small businesses have been sold the leftovers of the health insurance market,” said Nikhil Aggarwal, chief executive and co-founder of Corridor.
His company launched its AI benefits brokerage on Monday with $25m. Its plan is to change that with agents.
Bain Capital Ventures led the round. BoxGroup and Definition Capital took part. So did a long list of angel investors, whom the company describes in its announcement as founders and executives from OpenAI, Modal, Ramp, Scale AI, Oscar, Rogo, Decagon, Medallion, Reducto and Tennr. Dominic-Madori Davis reported the round for TechCrunch, which also carries the founders’ account of how the company started.
Why small companies get the leftovers
Corridor describes the gap it is aiming at as a question of economics rather than technology. A 20-person account earns a brokerage a fraction of what a large enterprise account earns. The work of quoting it, placing it and supporting it through the year is much the same. That has meant less help comparing plans, less strategic guidance and less support for employees, the company says.
“Administrative cost is the part of a premium that buys no care, and insurance distribution is where much of it accumulates because the work is still manual,” said Ryan Kim, a partner at Bain Capital Ventures, in a statement.
Corridor’s agents do that work, he said. Every employer then gets a quote against the full market, and carriers have to compete on price.
Corridor cites figures from KFF’s 2025 employer health benefits survey. People at small businesses pay 57% higher deductibles than employees at large companies, it says, often for worse cover. Only about half of small employers offer health benefits at all.
Corridor sells to companies with one to 500 employees. Each client gets a dedicated licensed advisor. The company says its clients are already saving an average of 20% on health benefits, without compromising on quality. Its customers run from technology and hospitality to physical therapy, wealth management and dental practices.
What the agents actually do
The advisor stays human. The agents take the paperwork.
An owner describes their team, budget and goals on a short form or a call. Agents then organise the company and plan data and gather quotes. They compare options across carriers, build proposals and flag risks. They also support enrolment and coordinate with the carriers themselves. The advisor returns with options, and employees pick from those.
The agents keep working after a company picks its plan, Aggarwal told TechCrunch. They check whether a doctor sits inside a customer’s network. They schedule care, and they send doctors updated insurance information.
“We are every single employee and management’s concierge for all things healthcare,” he said.
Money has been moving into this ground for months. TNW has covered rounds for agents in law, for health admin, for health insurance platforms and for European insurtech.
A running accident, and a pitch that changed shape
The founding account comes from TechCrunch. Jackson Wagner left a product lead role at Scale AI in July 2022. A running accident hurt him soon after. The handling of his care led to “significant, consistent, chronic pain”, he told TechCrunch.
“I developed a long list of complications that needed to be worked through one by one,” he said.
Wagner went on to a master’s degree at UC Berkeley. He then worked with Eric Qian, a former Scale AI colleague. Their startup, Capernaum AI, built a clinical agent for musculoskeletal care and chronic pain. The two approached an investor called Cold Start about funding it.
Aggarwal was a partner at Cold Start, as was Jason Dong. Aggarwal saw a larger opportunity than the one they pitched, TechCrunch reported. The four then left and started Corridor together. Aggarwal previously led growth at the ICHRA platform Venteur, according to the company, and built more than 250 brokerage partnerships there. Dong co-founded the pharma payments business Mural Health.
“Since health plans are the window through which the vast majority of Americans access health care, it became overwhelmingly clear that one of the highest impact things I could do to improve outcomes for individuals was to create a way for them to access better health plans,” Wagner told TechCrunch.
Timing, and who else is here
Corridor is not alone on this ground. TechCrunch names Ignition Benefits and Nava Benefits as companies working it.
Aggarwal told TechCrunch that 80% of small businesses choose their health plan in the fourth quarter. The company is now preparing for it. That quarter begins in October.
“Our vision is to build the most trusted healthcare institution in America,” he told TechCrunch. “To earn that, we are laser-focused on a simple promise: doing what we say we’re going to do for the businesses and employees we serve.”

articles.title: Women Still Face Too Much Bullshit—in Silicon Valley and Beyond
articles.text:
It didn’t take more than a few sessions for my new therapist to ask me a delicate question.
“Katie … do you have a problem with men?”
I wanted to say no. After all, brilliant, kind, fantastic men have long surrounded me at home and at work. The therapist in question was himself a man, and one I didn’t think twice about confiding in.
But if I’m being honest with myself, my therapist, and you? I do have a problem with some men. And it started with WIRED. In 2009, I got my first job interning and later reporting for WIRED.com. The publication in that era was enthusiastic about technology, and about the innovators and visionaries defining the future. For decades, WIRED eagerly reinforced the narrative that the vast majority of those geniuses were men: One 2010 analysis found that since its founding in 1993, WIRED had published 70 covers featuring at least one man. In that same span, the magazine published four covers—yes, four—that celebrate women for their professional accomplishments. I can’t remember working with a single female editor during my first stint at WIRED. I do, however, remember a 40-something male editor asking “where’d the legs go?” when I opted to wear pants instead of a skirt to the office.
It turned out to be just a preview. Off the top of my head, and across a 17-year career: There was the boss who, upon learning that I wanted kids, said that I seemed “too cold” to be a parent. I held my tears long enough to make it to the bathroom. A few years later, I remember being visibly pregnant in another employer’s office, as he joked that a woman as intense as me would probably keep her baby locked in a closet. One boss tried to pay me exponentially less than my male predecessor, because, he said, I was younger and less authoritative. A highly regarded media company enrolled me in its internal program for promising female leaders, which was being run by two male executives. I stood last year among a crowd of my peers at a packed event, listening to a prominent think-tank leader (male) credit WIRED’s previous editor in chief (also male) with the magazine’s successes during my tenure. Let’s not forget the cofounder of this very publication, who suggested via email following the 2024 election that I might “seppuku” myself because he disagreed with an editor’s letter I’d written. And in 2023, The New York Times published a story about my appointment as WIRED’s global editorial director—then had to issue a correction for inaccurately stating that I was the first woman to run the magazine. In fact, Katrina Heron ran WIRED from 1997 to 2001.
It’s gotten easier to be an ambitious woman, but if my own personal experience is any indication, not by nearly enough. The steady reminders of sexism and deeply ingrained gender dynamics have had consequences: I wonder, often, if I was granted certain jobs or opportunities for less-than-professional reasons; on the flip side, I also wonder if I got them to fulfill some kind of quota. I second-guess my decisions. I apologize endlessly. For years, I dressed as sloppily as possible—it was easier to show up unprofessionally than risk attracting any attention. In a bid to command the respect at work that a man would, I’ve often felt the need to behave more like a stereotypical one: meaner, louder, less empathetic. I hate that. And I’ve got it relatively easy: If a white, straight woman working in media and technology deals with this much bullshit, imagine the experience of a woman who happens to be a person of color, or gay, or transgender.
WIRED Women started as a joke at our weekly San Francisco happy hour; we laughed at the idea of turning a historically dude-loving publication into a women’s rag, complete with over-the-top pink design and outrageous cover lines—a tongue-in-cheek way to highlight the sorry state of women’s advancement in fields like tech and science. We soon found ourselves inspired, full of ideas, and ultimately pretty damn angry. But could we do it? Should we? Deciding in 2026 to commit an entire issue to all things women might seem regressive, or too obvious, or even unnecessary in an era where many people—and plenty in tech—are happy to wave off the notion that gender is still “a thing” to contend with.
I disagree. A convicted sex predator, after all, is in the White House; the tech industry executives in his ear are virtually all men. Women do wield power in Silicon Valley, but far too many still serve at the pleasure of a man above them. When Mark Zuckerberg bemoans the loss of “masculine energy” in his workforce, and Pete Hegseth says that the military is too “effeminate,” and Elon Musk’s DOGE cuts impact Black female civil servants above all other groups—it can seem like they want to erase women altogether. And it’s infuriating. The world deserves better heroes, women deserve better colleagues, and my daughter—who sleeps in a bed, not a locked closet—deserves to be less furious than I am when she’s 40. My therapist, God bless him, was onto something.
